title: Samurai Executioner
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: An episodic Edo-period gekiga by the Lone Wolf and Cub team: Yamada Asaemon tests the Shogun's blades and beheads condemned criminals, and each story looks at a crime and the person behind it (Dark Horse blurb; ANN review of volume 7). Later stories follow a police officer hunting a serial killer alongside Asaemon (ANN). Dark Horse's own blurb promises blood, torture and 'the evil prevalent in human failure.'
life_message: It holds up a stoic, merciful discipline: doing a grim duty with full attention while reflecting honestly on life, death and justice.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Asaemon's office serves the Shogun's law, but samurai honor and revenge drive many criminals (blurb 'vengeance').

Order vs freedom.evidence: Rigid Edo legal order; executions enforce everyone's place.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Stories weigh family ties of criminals against public law (to verify).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Shogunate rank structure; Asaemon serves loyally under the Shogun.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Sword tradition 'thick in tradition' (Dark Horse blurb); Buddhist-tinged mortality.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival-level poverty and crime in Edo (MU Commoner/s).

folkways.japan: Set in Edo-period Japan, it reflects samurai service, hereditary roles and public execution as the period's norms, described here as historical context.

delivery.evidence: ANN review: reflection on life and death arises from each story and its emotional weight, not lectures.

personified.ideology: stoic duty carried out with mercy

delivery.note: Criminals are often given understandable motives, while the system of execution itself is rarely questioned (to verify).

winners_losers: The law and Asaemon's blade always prevail; condemned criminals lose but are often given sympathy and a human story.
